blocks.text: The Sudoku Solver problem asks you to fill a 9 by 9 grid so that every row, every column, and every 3 by 3 sub-box contains the digits 1 through 9 exactly once, given a partially filled starting grid with some cells already fixed and the rest empty.

This is a direct, practical application of the same choose, explore, unchoose backtracking rhythm used throughout this course, applied to a genuinely useful real problem: find an empty cell, try each digit that does not immediately violate a constraint, recurse, and if a dead end is reached, undo and try the next digit.

Sudoku puzzles that are designed to have a unique solution solve very fast in practice, even though the raw worst case search space is enormous, because the row, column, and box constraints prune the vast majority of candidate digits at almost every cell.

The same choose, explore, unchoose skeleton used for Permutations, Combinations, and N Queens applies here unchanged, only the definition of "candidate" (a digit 1 through 9) and "valid" (passes the row, column, and box checks) differ. Recognizing this shared skeleton across seemingly unrelated problems is the actual skill being tested by backtracking questions, not memorizing Sudoku specifically.

blocks.caption: A candidate digit at a given cell must avoid conflicts across three overlapping zones: its row, its column, and its 3x3 box.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406864482-540622498.png

For a candidate digit at position (row, col), it is valid only if that digit does not already appear anywhere else in that row, that column, or that cell's 3 by 3 sub-box. The row and column checks are a straightforward scan of 9 cells each. The sub-box check requires computing which of the nine 3 by 3 boxes the cell belongs to.

The box arithmetic: the top left corner of the box containing (row, col) is at (row divided by 3, rounded down, times 3, col divided by 3, rounded down, times 3). In C++ with integer division this is simply (row / 3) * 3 and (col / 3) * 3, since integer division automatically truncates toward zero for non negative values, giving the correct box origin directly.

The single line if (solve(board)) return true; is what makes this an efficient single-solution solver: as soon as any recursive call finds a complete, valid solution, that true propagates immediately back up through every level of recursion, stopping the search instantly instead of continuing to look for additional solutions that Sudoku, by design, does not have.

blocks.caption: Placing digits cell by cell, hitting a dead end where no digit is valid, backtracking to the previous cell, and trying its next candidate digit.
blocks.text: /engineering/dsa-media/1785406864482-542777050.png

Consider a simplified trace: the solver places 5 in an empty cell, moves to the next empty cell and successfully places another digit, but several cells later reaches a cell where none of 1 through 9 pass isValid, every digit conflicts with something already placed. This triggers return false from that cell's loop, which propagates back to the PREVIOUS cell's call, undoing its placement (board[row][col] = '.') and trying the next digit there instead. This is backtracking exactly as defined earlier in this course: choose, explore, and on failure, unchoose and try the next option.

In the absolute worst case, with m empty cells and up to 9 candidate digits at each, an extremely loose upper bound is 9^m. In practice this bound is wildly pessimistic: the row, column, and box constraints eliminate the overwhelming majority of the 9 candidates at almost every cell, especially as the grid fills in and more constraints become active, which is exactly why real Sudoku puzzles solve in a fraction of a second despite the frightening theoretical bound.

This gap between the theoretical worst case and the practical runtime is worth stating explicitly in an interview: it demonstrates you understand that backtracking's real world performance depends heavily on how aggressively the constraints prune the search, not just on the raw size of the search space.

content.title: 5. A Stronger Heuristic: Most Constrained Cell First

blocks.text: The implementation above always scans cells in a fixed left to right, top to bottom order. A meaningfully stronger version instead chooses, at every step, the EMPTY CELL WITH THE FEWEST valid candidate digits remaining, often called the "most constrained variable" heuristic. Filling in the cell that has the least freedom first causes dead ends to be discovered much earlier in the search, before large numbers of digits have been placed downstream on top of an eventually doomed choice.

The intuition: if a cell only has one valid candidate digit left, filling it immediately either confirms progress or reveals a contradiction right away, either outcome is more useful than spending time on a cell with 6 open candidates whose eventual failure would only be discovered many cells later, after much more wasted work.

This heuristic requires recomputing, at each step, which remaining empty cell currently has the fewest valid candidates, adding bookkeeping overhead per step but often reducing the total number of cells explored so significantly that it is a net win, particularly on harder puzzles with fewer initially filled cells.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Cell selection strategy","When dead ends are discovered","Typical performance"],"rows":[["Fixed left to right, top to bottom","Often late, after many downstream cells are filled on a doomed branch","Correct, simplest to implement"],["Most constrained cell first","Early, since a cell with one or zero candidates reveals problems immediately","Correct, meaningfully faster on harder puzzles"]]}

blocks.text: Recomputing the full row, column, and box scan naively every single time instead of maintaining incremental "used digit" sets per row, column, and box: this still produces correct output, and is what the reference implementation above does for clarity, but a production quality solver typically maintains nine row sets, nine column sets, and nine box sets updated incrementally for better performance.

Forgetting the early return true propagation: without it, the solver keeps searching for additional solutions after already finding one, which is both unnecessary (valid Sudoku puzzles have a unique solution) and can turn a fast solve into an extremely slow one.

Getting the sub-box math wrong: a common slip is writing row % 3 instead of row / 3, or forgetting to multiply back by 3 after the division, both of which produce a box index that does not correspond to the correct 3 by 3 region.

Mutating the board without a working unchoose path on every exit: if a bug causes a specific code path to return without resetting board[row][col] back to empty, the board is left in a corrupted state that silently breaks every subsequent branch of the search, often producing confusing partial output rather than a clean failure.
Sudoku Solver: the direct application, fill in a partially completed valid grid to a full solution using backtracking.

Valid Sudoku: a simpler, non backtracking variant, given a grid (which may be only partially filled and does not need solving), just verify it does not currently violate the row, column, or box constraints. This reuses the exact same three zone conflict checking idea without any search or recursion at all.

items: Can you derive the sub-box index arithmetic (row/3, col/3, scaled back by 3) from scratch rather than memorizing it?
Can you explain exactly why the early return true is necessary once a solution is found?
Can you explain why the theoretical 9^m worst case bound is a poor predictor of real world Sudoku solving time?
Can you describe the most constrained cell heuristic and why filling low candidate cells first tends to find dead ends faster?
